subject: sociology
chapter_title: Social Structure, Stratification and Social Processes in Society

concepts.title: Social Structure: Stable Patterns of Relationships
concepts.definition: Social structure refers to the recurring, organised patterns by which a society arranges its members -- families, castes, classes, offices and the expected relations among them. It is invisible as a thing yet visible in effects: it channels what people routinely do and constrains what they can do.
concepts.key_idea: Society has a skeleton -- positions and relations laid out in advance -- and everyone is born into its frame.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy201.txt lines 1-120 (introduction, social structure as organised pattern, constraining individual action, examples of structure in daily life)

solution_steps.explain: Behind repeated behaviour -- who defers to whom, who marries whom -- lies an organised arrangement of positions.
Structure precedes each individual: options, roles and life chances arrive pre-sorted.

solution_steps.action: see the constraint and the scope
solution_steps.explain: Structure constrains without dictating; individuals work within, around and occasionally against it.

concepts.title: Social Stratification: Caste and Class
concepts.definition: Stratification is society's ranking of people into layers with unequal wealth, power and honour. Caste is ascribed at birth, bounded by endogamy, backed by ideas of purity and pollution, and traditionally unchangeable; class is based mainly on economic position, is theoretically open to mobility, and is reproduced through property and education rather than ritual.
concepts.key_idea: Caste fixes your floor at birth; class can shift with fortune -- both stack society into layers of unequal life chances.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy201.txt lines 120-280 (social stratification, caste and class as forms of stratification, features of caste system, class systems, openness and mobility, ritual status)
question_patterns: distinguish caste from class as systems of stratification
in class 11 social structure and stratification: what are the main features of the caste system
why is caste said to be based on ritual purity and pollution
can class position change across generations
explain how caste and class interact in modern india
define social stratification and give its characteristics

solution_steps.explain: Caste ranks by birth and ritual status; class ranks by economic resources and market position.
Caste walls itself in by endogamy and prescribed contact rules; class boundaries are porous and negotiable.
Individual caste is unchangeable though the group may claim higher rank; class position can change with income, education or loss.
In India caste and class overlap -- ritual rank historically correlated with property, and the overlap persists unevenly.

worked_examples.q: Which is fixed at birth: caste or class?

concepts.title: Social Processes: Cooperation, Competition and Conflict
concepts.definition: Social life runs on recurrent processes of interaction. Cooperation joins efforts toward shared goals; competition is the rule-bound race for scarce goods where rivals chase the same prize; conflict is the collision where parties seek to nullify each other. Societies blend all three, often in sequence.
concepts.key_idea: Working together, racing each other, clashing head-on -- cooperation, competition and conflict are society's three basic gears.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy201.txt lines 280-400 (social processes, cooperation, competition, conflict, accomodation and assimilation mentions)
question_patterns: explain cooperation competition and conflict as social processes
in class 11 social structure and stratification: how can competition turn into conflict
give an example of cooperation at the family and national level
how does conflict lead to social change
distinguish competition from conflict with examples

solution_steps.explain: Where goals are joint -- harvesting a field, running a festival -- cooperation organises the effort.
Where goods are scarce and rules recognised -- exams, markets, elections -- competition orders the rivalry.
Where rules break down and parties aim at each other, conflict erupts; its settlement often produces new arrangements.

worked_examples.q: Joining efforts toward shared goals is called what?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A successful entrepreneur from a traditionally artisan caste rises in wealth but faces rejection from elite clubs. Explain what this case shows about caste and class.

solution_template.explain: Wealth and enterprise lifted his class position -- the economic layer moved.
Exclusion from elite clubs shows ritual status still policing social distance -- the caste layer resisted.
Caste and class are distinct but intertwined systems; money can buy some goods and not others.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Two shopkeepers first compete for customers, then agree on prices together, and finally fight over a shared parking space. Classify each phase as a social process.

solution_template.explain: Rivals chasing the same customers within market rules is competition.
Jointly fixing prices shows cooperation -- shared action toward a common goal (though it may be unlawful collusion).
Fighting over the space, each aiming to defeat the other, is conflict -- the same relationship cycling through all three processes.
